## 📖 The Internet Archive, in cards

The archive is not only the Wayback Machine. **Two types of cards are built so far:**

- **📖 IA Book** — a scanned book, page by page: turn, zoom, **search inside it** (each hit names its page and shows the matched words boxed on the page), read that page's OCR text, open the PDF/EPUB/OCR. Both books open in **facing-pages mode**, full width — the board sets that (⚙ Reading mode), and the ▭ button on a card overrides it for you. Leaf 1 alone is the cover, so turn one page to see a spread; **⇥** pairs the cover instead, for scans that start on a text page. Flip between the two books: a **16-page** illustrated children's book and a **304-page** Dostoevsky — the page count comes from the IIIF manifest, so both just work.
- **📦 IA Item** — any item by identifier, with its engagement views (all-time / 30-day / 7-day), file count and size, and thumbnail.

The four cards below are the media types the next three widgets will render — plain IA Item cards today:

- **🎬 a Prelinger film** — 888 MB, and the source of the keyframe filmstrip
- **🎧 a Live Music Archive concert** — 20 tracks, each with its own spectrogram
- **🎧 a LibriVox audiobook** — 7 chapters, and it carries its own scanned book
- **🗂️ MIT OpenCourseWare** — 511 courses of titled, timed, captioned lectures

**And the media plays.** The two player cards at the bottom stream the real files — an 11-minute Prelinger film and three LibriVox chapters as a playlist — straight from `archive.org/download/`. That needed no new widget: the player now accepts a direct media URL and builds the row without any API call. Range requests mean seeking works.

Build order for the rest of the family: **IA Playlist → IA Video + filmstrip → IA Audio** — see `docs/INTERNET-ARCHIVE.md`.

config.annotation: **About Bananas** (1935, Prelinger) — the whole 11-minute film, streamed straight from `archive.org/download/`. The archive serves Range requests, so you can seek.
**The Art of War**, read for LibriVox — three chapters as a playlist, each streamed from the archive. No API call was needed to play these: a direct URL *is* the media.
